original.title: Outline of a Theory of Practice

core_idea: Social life is made of practices: routinized ways of doing and saying that combine bodies, objects, know-how and shared meanings. Instead of explaining behaviour by what is in individual minds or by abstract structures, practice theory studies what people actually do, again and again, and how that reproduces or changes social order. Bourdieu's version adds habitus (embodied dispositions) and fields (arenas of struggle).
key_concepts_note: Use the concepts already stored for this theory in the library (theories.concepts).
when_to_use: How is an everyday practice (teaching, farming, cooking, commuting, consuming) carried out, learned and changed?
Why do routines persist even when people say they want to change them?
How is work in an organization actually done, as opposed to how it is described?
Typical data: observation, ethnography, interviews about doing, diaries, video.
common_mistakes: Studying only what people say about a practice, not the doing itself.
Treating 'practice' as a synonym for 'behaviour' or 'activity' without its elements (materials, competences, meanings).
Using Bourdieu and Schatzki interchangeably; they are different versions.
